title: QEMU Core Dump and Persistent Zombie Detection
exclusions: Detects systemd-coredump records for an explicitly approved QEMU executable and QEMU processes whose `/proc/<pid>/stat` state is `Z` in at least two collector observations spanning 45 seconds. It does not infer every abnormal VM stop, guest panic, clean shutdown, hung but non-zombie process, libvirt daemon failure, missing VM, or root cause. Hosts without systemd-coredump need a separately designed crash source. Executable allow-lists, domain attribution, the local index/source type, 60-second poll, 45-second persistence rule, inventory, and exceptions are deployment choices. The UC does not enable core storage, collect core contents, restart a VM, kill/reap a process, or prove service restoration.
evidence: After deployment, retain the `qemu_core_dump_or_persistent_zombie` saved-search definition, ACL, one-minute schedule, dispatch rows, alerts, and dashboard state; signed collector source/hash and effective input; raw normalized crash or process observations; systemd journal metadata and permitted libvirt domain log excerpt; `qemu_process_inventory.csv` and `qemu_process_exceptions.csv` revisions; fixed control results; incident/change records; and a later healthy domain/process observation. These artifacts document search behavior, not runtime validation. This review executed no QEMU crash, zombie, collector, search, alert, restart, or recovery test.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Fix search time at 2026-07-29T01:00:00Z. In an isolated index, ingest one valid `event_kind=coredump` event at 00:58 for `host=kvm-lab-01`, `pid=4102`, `process_name=qemu-system-x86_64`, approved `process_exe=/usr/libexec/qemu-kvm`, `signal_name=SIGSEGV`, `coredump_id=boot-a:4102:1785286680000000`, and complete schema/run/hash fields; expect one `qemu_core_dump` row. Separately ingest valid `process_snapshot` events at 00:58:30 and 00:59:30 for the same host, PID, `process_start_ticks=987654`, executable, and `process_state=Z`; expect one `persistent_qemu_zombie` row with `observations=2` and `observation_span_seconds=60`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and require zero rows: a QEMU process in `S` or `R`; only one zombie observation; two zombie observations 30 seconds apart; repeated PID with different `process_start_ticks`; coredump for an unapproved executable; QEMU journal text without a systemd-coredump event; missing/invalid schema, observed epoch, run ID, collector hash, PID, event kind, or crash ID; event older than 15 minutes; host absent or inactive in inventory; and an exact active exception. An expired exception must not suppress. A missing collector run or systemd-coredump source must appear in companion source-health coverage, never as a healthy QEMU result.

dataSources: A deployment-owned signed scripted input on each Linux KVM host emits `sourcetype=linux:qemu_process_health` into local `index=virtualization`; both names are local conventions. Every 60 seconds it reads documented `/proc/<pid>/stat` process state/start identity for approved QEMU executables and incrementally exports systemd-coredump journal metadata such as `COREDUMP_PID`, `COREDUMP_EXE`, `COREDUMP_SIGNAL_NAME`, and `COREDUMP_TIMESTAMP`. Required normalized fields are `_time, _indextime, host, event_kind, schema_version, observed_epoch, pid, process_name, process_exe, process_state, process_start_ticks, signal_name, coredump_id, domain_name, run_id, collector_sha256`. A Splunk Universal Forwarder (Splunkbase 617) runs the input; no vendor add-on supplies this custom schema.
app: A version-controlled deployment app provides the signed read-only QEMU process/systemd-coredump collector, `[script://...]` input, local field contract, inventory and exception lookups, source-health search, alert, dashboard, fixtures, and runbook. A supported Splunk Universal Forwarder (Splunkbase 617) runs it on each scoped host. This custom feed is not a documented default of the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux.
spl:
index=virtualization sourcetype="linux:qemu_process_health" earliest=-15m@m
| eval schema_version=tonumber(schema_version), observed_epoch=tonumber(observed_epoch), pid=tonumber(pid), process_start_ticks=tonumber(process_start_ticks), event_kind=lower(trim(event_kind)), process_state=upper(trim(process_state)), process_exe=trim(process_exe)
| where schema_version=1 AND observed_epoch>0 AND pid>0 AND in(event_kind,"coredump","process_snapshot") AND len(process_name)>0 AND len(process_exe)>0 AND len(run_id)>0 AND len(collector_sha256)>0
| lookup qemu_process_inventory.csv host process_exe OUTPUT monitor_enabled owner service_name runbook monitor_from_epoch monitor_until_epoch
| eval monitor_from_epoch=tonumber(monitor_from_epoch), monitor_until_epoch=tonumber(monitor_until_epoch), inventory_active=if(lower(trim(monitor_enabled))="true" AND monitor_from_epoch<=now() AND monitor_until_epoch>now(),1,0)
| where inventory_active=1
| eval entity_key=case(event_kind="coredump" AND len(coredump_id)>0,"crash:".host.":".coredump_id,event_kind="process_snapshot" AND process_start_ticks>0,"process:".host.":".pid.":".process_start_ticks)
| where len(entity_key)>0 AND ((event_kind="coredump" AND len(signal_name)>0) OR (event_kind="process_snapshot" AND process_state="Z"))
| stats earliest(observed_epoch) as first_observed_epoch latest(observed_epoch) as last_observed_epoch count as observations latest(_indextime) as _indextime latest(event_kind) as event_kind latest(pid) as pid latest(process_name) as process_name latest(process_exe) as process_exe latest(process_state) as process_state latest(signal_name) as signal_name latest(coredump_id) as coredump_id latest(domain_name) as domain_name latest(run_id) as run_id latest(collector_sha256) as collector_sha256 latest(owner) as owner latest(service_name) as service_name latest(runbook) as runbook by host entity_key
| eval observation_span_seconds=last_observed_epoch-first_observed_epoch, alert_reason=case(event_kind="coredump","qemu_core_dump",event_kind="process_snapshot" AND observations>=2 AND observation_span_seconds>=45,"persistent_qemu_zombie")
| where len(alert_reason)>0
| lookup qemu_process_exceptions.csv host entity_key alert_reason OUTPUT exception_until_epoch reason AS exception_reason ticket exception_owner
| eval exception_until_epoch=tonumber(exception_until_epoch), exception_active=if(exception_until_epoch>now() AND len(exception_reason)>0 AND len(ticket)>0,1,0)
| where exception_active=0
| eval use_case_id="UC-2.3.9", detection_semantics="documented_coredump_or_persistent_proc_zombie_not_all_qemu_failures"
| table first_observed_epoch last_observed_epoch _indextime host domain_name pid process_name process_exe process_state signal_name coredump_id observations observation_span_seconds alert_reason owner service_name runbook run_id collector_sha256 entity_key detection_semantics use_case_id
| sort 0 -last_observed_epoch host pid
description: Detects one fresh row per inventory-approved QEMU systemd-coredump record and one row per QEMU process identity observed in Linux zombie state in at least two one-minute polls spanning 45 seconds. Crash rows are keyed by core-dump identity; zombie rows are keyed by host, PID, and process start ticks to resist PID reuse.
value: Separating documented crash evidence from persistent process-reaping failure gives virtualization responders a defensible starting point for preserving diagnostics, checking domain impact, and restoring service. Explicit source-health and identity rules prevent ordinary QEMU log wording or a recycled PID from becoming a false crash claim.
implementation: Deploy a signed least-privilege collector through a version-controlled Universal Forwarder app. Poll approved QEMU executables every 60 seconds, export `/proc` state with process start identity, and checkpoint only systemd-coredump metadata—never core contents. Validate executable paths, journal access, PID reuse, timestamps, field types, and domain attribution on each host cohort. Schedule the SPL every minute over 15 minutes, alert immediately for a new core-dump identity or after two zombie observations spanning at least 45 seconds, and run separate inventory-first checks for missing/stale/error data. Preserve diagnostics and use the virtualization runbook; do not restart, kill, or reap from SPL.
visualization: Place expected-host collector freshness, journal checkpoint health, invalid schema/hash, and duplicate-run coverage first. Then show new QEMU core dumps by signal/executable/domain and persistent zombies by host, PID, start identity, observations, and age. Drill down to the normalized raw event, permitted systemd-coredump metadata, domain log, inventory, exception, incident, and later recovery evidence. Do not label absence of a row as QEMU or VM health.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. No accelerated CIM dataset is asserted to preserve systemd-coredump identity, `/proc` process state/start ticks, executable allow-list, collector schema/run/hash, or two-observation persistence semantics. The custom event remains primary.

knownFalsePositives:
A matching row is evidence of either a core-dump record or a persistent zombie process identity; it is not by itself proof of root cause, data loss, or current VM outage.

1. **Approved QEMU/libvirt failure-injection test** — A lab, chaos, crash-handler, or support reproduction can intentionally terminate QEMU and create a real systemd-coredump record. Verify exact host/domain, test plan, executable/build, signal, change ticket, owner, start/end, and evidence-retention requirement. Use the `lookup qemu_process_exceptions.csv` mechanism only for the exact `host,entity_key,alert_reason` with reason, ticket, owner, and UTC expiry; retain the event on the dashboard.

2. **Vendor or platform qualification crash** — Upgrade validation may deliberately reproduce a known QEMU defect. Match package/build, domain fixture, core-dump ID, issue/support case, and bounded test window. Do not suppress all QEMU crashes by executable or package version.

3. **Transient zombie awaiting normal parent reaping** — A terminated child can briefly show state `Z` before its parent collects status. Confirm the same PID and `process_start_ticks` across observations, parent PID/state, and a newer snapshot. The 45-second/two-poll rule intentionally filters a single observation; tune only from measured collector jitter and host behavior.

4. **Stale or duplicated collector output** — A replayed scripted-input batch can manufacture apparent persistence. Compare `run_id`, `collector_sha256`, observed and index times, forwarder instance, and effective input assignment. Repair collection; never use a broad process exception to hide duplicate runs.

5. **Executable allow-list or domain-attribution error** — A wrapper, renamed binary, session QEMU, test emulator, or stale PID-to-domain map can be classified incorrectly. Verify `/proc/<pid>/exe`, process start identity, cgroup/libvirt metadata, domain XML/log, and inventory revision. Correct the exact inventory mapping and replay fixtures before closing.

6. **Core metadata retained after service recovery** — The coredump record remains valid even if HA or an operator already restored the VM. Correlate domain state, replacement process start, guest/service checks, and incident timeline. Deduplicate on `coredump_id`; do not suppress future crashes merely because recovery was fast.

**Suppression mechanism:** `qemu_process_exceptions.csv` is exact on `host,entity_key,alert_reason` and requires future numeric `exception_until_epoch`, nonempty reason, approved ticket, and owner. It suppresses notification only. Expired/malformed exceptions, new core-dump IDs, different process start identities, source-health gaps, schema/hash drift, and duplicate collection remain visible.
reviewer: documentation-only Cursor AI editorial review against libvirt QEMU core-dump/debug-log guidance, systemd-coredump metadata, Linux `/proc/<pid>/stat` process identity/state, and Splunk scripted-input/scheduled-alert documentation; QEMU/libvirt/Linux/forwarder/Splunk versions, collector permissions and parsing, crash and zombie generation, fixtures, source health, alert delivery, diagnostics, restart/reaping, and production recovery were specified but not executed or QEMU/libvirt/Linux/Splunk/virtualization-owner/SME signed
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact detection boundary

Assign virtualization, Linux platform, Splunk data/content, workload, incident, and evidence owners. Inventory supported KVM hosts, approved QEMU executable paths, domain attribution method, service owner, and runbook. Use supported QEMU, libvirt, systemd, Linux, and Universal Forwarder releases qualified by the deployment. This review ran no version combination, so it asserts no `splunkVersions`. The collector identity needs read access only to required `/proc` entries and permitted systemd journal metadata; it does not need VM lifecycle, signal, debugger, core-content, or configuration-write privilege. Restrict app, inventory, exception, and checkpoint writes.

The two signals are deliberately separate. systemd-coredump documents `COREDUMP_PID`, `COREDUMP_EXE`, `COREDUMP_SIGNAL_NAME`, `COREDUMP_TIMESTAMP`, and related metadata for a crashed process when that facility handles the dump. Linux `/proc/<pid>/stat` documents process state `Z` and start time. A zombie is already terminated and awaits parent reaping; it is not a running QEMU consuming ordinary guest CPU. Libvirt documents domain logs and core-dump investigation, but arbitrary strings such as `terminated`, `warning`, or `killed` are not a universal crash schema. Do not make them primary predicates.

## Step 1 — Build the read-only normalized collector

Create a signed collector in a deployment-owned app. Every 60 seconds enumerate only processes whose resolved `/proc/<pid>/exe` exactly matches an active inventory path. Read PID, parent PID, command name, state, and start ticks from documented proc interfaces without shell `grep` pipelines. Emit one flat `event_kind=process_snapshot` record per approved QEMU process with `schema_version=1`, host, observed epoch, PID, executable, state, start ticks, optional domain attribution, run ID, and collector SHA-256. Treat process disappearance during reads, permission denial, malformed proc data, and inventory mismatch as bounded collector-health events, not zombie records.

Incrementally query the local systemd journal for new coredump entries and checkpoint by stable cursor or an equivalently tested monotonic mechanism. Emit only metadata needed for triage as `event_kind=coredump`; construct `coredump_id` from stable source identity such as boot ID, coredump PID, and coredump timestamp. Require an exact approved `COREDUMP_EXE` path. Do not copy `COREDUMP`, stack traces, guest memory, command-line secrets, or core files into the operational index. Hosts where another core handler is configured are explicitly uncovered until a source-specific collector is designed.

Resolve `domain_name` only with a tested local mapping, for example libvirt machine cgroup/domain metadata. Preserve null when attribution is uncertain. Never infer a domain solely from PID reuse or an unescaped command-line substring. Record package/build and domain UUID in the raw event if locally approved, but do not make undocumented fields search prerequisites.

Configure a local scripted input such as `[script://$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA_qemu_process_health/bin/collect_qemu_health]` with `interval=60`, local `index=virtualization`, and local `sourcetype=linux:qemu_process_health`. The exact path and names are deployment conventions. Sign, peer-review, hash-pin, and protect the collector; measure runtime, journal volume, event size, CPU, memory, and forwarder queue impact.

## Step 2 — Govern inventory, fields, and source health

Create `qemu_process_inventory.csv` keyed by exact `host,process_exe` with `monitor_enabled,owner,service_name,runbook,monitor_from_epoch,monitor_until_epoch`. Reject wildcards, duplicate active rows, relative paths, and invalid epochs. Reconcile the list against libvirt host inventory and actual resolved executable paths after package or platform changes.

Create `qemu_process_exceptions.csv` keyed by exact `host,entity_key,alert_reason` with finite `exception_until_epoch,reason,ticket,exception_owner`. The `entity_key` is `crash:<host>:<coredump_id>` for a crash and `process:<host>:<pid>:<process_start_ticks>` for a zombie. This precision prevents an approved test from muting a later process or crash.

Verify field extraction and types in `index=virtualization sourcetype=linux:qemu_process_health`: integer schema/epochs/PID/start ticks, lowercase event kind, uppercase process state, absolute executable, unique run/hash, and stable coredump ID. Compare process snapshots with `/proc` and `virsh list --all`; compare crash metadata with `coredumpctl info` only on an approved test host. A source-health search must start from expected inventory and report no collector run within two poll intervals, journal query/checkpoint error, denied proc reads, unexpected executable, schema/hash change, duplicate run, future time, indexing lag, and domain-map failure.

## Step 3 — Save and schedule the SPL

Save the supplied SPL as `qemu_core_dump_or_persistent_zombie`; schedule it every minute with a 15-minute lookback. The search validates schema and inventory before assigning identity. Every valid coredump record alerts once by `coredump_id`; every zombie needs at least two matching observations for the same host, PID, and process start ticks spanning 45 seconds. That persistence value is a starting anti-jitter rule, not a Linux or QEMU vendor threshold. Tune only after measuring poll completion and normal reaping latency.

Trigger per result and throttle on `entity_key,alert_reason`, while continuing dashboard updates. Route core dumps immediately to virtualization on-call and preserve diagnostics before rotation. Route persistent zombies to the Linux/virtualization owner with parent-process and domain context. Keep collection failures in a separate high-visibility alert; missing data is unknown, never healthy.

The SPL does not claim that every coredump caused guest outage or that a zombie remains harmful. Responders must establish domain state and impact. Do not add broad text alternatives unless a vendor/version-specific event contract and fixture prove them.

## Step 4 — Validate controls and failure behavior

Load the fixed positive scenarios into an isolated index and exact inventory. Assert one crash row and one persistent-zombie row with expected identities, counts, span, signal, owner, and semantics. Run every negative variant independently. Add boundaries at spans 44/45/46 seconds, one/two/three observations, PID reuse with changed start ticks, same coredump replay, two different core IDs, process state `X` or lowercase serialization, delayed indexing, future observed time, inventory start/end equality, exception expiry equality, and collector hash change.

On a nonproduction host, validate proc parsing against the same PID without creating a zombie. Validate coredump journal parsing against a pre-existing permitted non-QEMU fixture or an owner-approved QEMU test; do not crash production for evidence. Test no systemd-coredump handler, journal rotation, cursor invalidation, access denial, process exit during read, executable replacement, session versus system libvirt, domain rename, malformed event, forwarder outage, index denial, lookup replication, duplicate app assignment, and clock skew. Prove each source problem appears in coverage rather than the primary detector.

Keep `status=draft` until Linux, virtualization, workload, and Splunk owners accept versions, executable scope, permissions, privacy, collector/checkpoint behavior, identities, fixtures, source health, alert routing, diagnostic retention, and recovery procedure.

## Step 5 — Respond and preserve evidence safely

For a core-dump row: verify raw metadata and executable inventory; identify the domain without guessing; check current `virsh`/management state and guest/service impact; preserve permitted `coredumpctl` metadata, `/var/log/libvirt/qemu/<domain>.log`, libvirt daemon logs, package versions, domain XML, and incident timeline according to policy; consult the virtualization/vendor support path before deleting evidence; restore through approved HA or lifecycle tooling; and validate the new domain process and guest workload.

For a persistent zombie: verify repeated state and start identity, parent PID/state, domain mapping, and current libvirt view. A zombie cannot be repaired by sending it another signal. Escalate parent reaping or daemon behavior to the Linux/libvirt owner. Do not kill unrelated parent processes, restart libvirt globally, or reboot a host from this alert. Consider workload evacuation, quorum, storage, and change controls before any host action.

Close a crash only with documented current domain/workload state and retained root-cause evidence or support handoff. Close a zombie only after a newer collector run no longer shows that exact process identity and platform health is verified. Disappearance alone can follow host or collector failure, so require source freshness.

## Step 6 — Troubleshoot without broadening claims

- **No crash events:** confirm systemd-coredump is the configured handler, journal access, checkpoint/cursor, exact executable path, retention, and collector health. Do not substitute free-text syslog silently.
- **Zombie never alerts:** inspect raw state, start ticks, poll completion, process lifetime, and 45-second span. A single transient `Z` is intentionally excluded.
- **Repeated false persistence:** compare observed/index times, run IDs, forwarder/app assignment, checkpoint, and event replay. Repair duplicate ingestion.
- **Wrong domain:** verify cgroup/libvirt mapping and domain UUID against current process identity. Leave attribution null until proven.
- **QEMU exited without coredump:** this UC does not cover every exit. Review libvirt/QMP/domain lifecycle evidence and design a separately sourced condition if operationally required.
- **Core contents unavailable:** systemd may retain metadata after the external file is removed. The alert remains a valid metadata record but cannot promise a backtrace.
- **Alert after recovery:** deduplication records the crash; update incident state with current domain/workload evidence instead of suppressing the historic event.
- **Permission errors:** grant only narrowly reviewed journal/proc access or adjust the collector design. Never run arbitrary shell input as unrestricted root merely to satisfy monitoring.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for a virtual machine program that has crashed and left a core-dump record, or has finished but remains stuck waiting to be cleaned up. The alert helps operators preserve evidence and check the affected machine; it does not restart or kill anything.
